questions.prompt: Why do muscles work in pairs?
options: Bones are too heavy for one muscle
Muscles can only pull, so a second muscle is needed to move the bone back
questions.explain: Contracting muscles pull; they cannot push.

questions.prompt: What joins one bone to another at a joint?
Match each joint to where it is found.
questions.explain: Each type allows a different range of movement.

questions.prompt: Which joint lets your arm move in a full circle?
options: Ball and socket joint at the shoulder
questions.explain: A ball in a cup-shaped socket allows movement in all directions.

questions.prompt: What is the role of cartilage at the end of bones in a joint?
options: It reduces friction and absorbs shock
questions.explain: Smooth, slightly springy cartilage protects the bone ends.

questions.prompt: Which vitamin helps the body absorb calcium to build bones, and is made in the skin in sunlight?
questions.explain: Vitamin D deficiency can cause rickets in children.

questions.prompt: When you kick a football, your leg straightens at the knee. Which muscle contracts?
options: The quadriceps at the front of the thigh
The hamstrings at the back of the thigh
questions.explain: The quadriceps pulls the lower leg straight; the hamstrings bend the knee.

questions.prompt: Explain why the teenage years are especially important for building strong bones, and suggest two habits that help.
questions.modelAnswer: Most bone mass is built during childhood and the teenage years, reaching a peak in the early twenties; after that it slowly declines. Building more bone now means stronger bones and less risk of fractures and osteoporosis later in life. Habits: eating calcium-rich foods (milk, curd, ragi, leafy greens), getting some sunlight for vitamin D, and doing regular weight-bearing exercise such as running, skipping or sports.
rubric: Peak bone mass is built in the teens/early twenties
